title: AI Tools for Teachers, Rated
author: RatedEd
summary: RatedEd opens a rating series by arguing that schools waste money because purchasing processes reward good marketing over good products. It scores AI tools for teachers on five criteria: value per dollar, ease of implementation, evidence of impact, teacher time saved, and transparency. Planning tools such as MagicSchool, Diffit, Brisk, Eduaide and Curipod are rated highly, with generic ChatGPT given a middling score. In the grading section, Brisk feedback features and Khanmigo score well while AI essay graders are called overhyped. The piece concludes that districts err by mandating a single tool for everyone and recommends a free stack of three tools. It is a practical, opinionated consumer guide to classroom AI products, which is why it sits in Ed-Tech.
points: Districts waste money because purchasing rewards marketing over evidence, so the author proposes a five-criterion rubric (value, ease, evidence, time saved, transparency).
Tools that live inside teachers existing workflows (Brisk in Google Docs, MagicSchool free tier, Diffit leveling) earn the top ratings.
AI essay graders are rated overhyped because feedback is generic, cannot judge voice or argument, and students learn to game it.
Khanmigo is framed as an AI tutor that makes grading easier by improving work before submission, rather than a grader.
The biggest purchasing mistake is mandating one tool district-wide instead of letting different teachers choose different solutions.
quotes: This is how schools waste money. Not through incompetence, but through a purchasing process that rewards good marketing over good products.
Paste any text, topic, or YouTube URL and Diffit generates leveled versions with vocabulary support and comprehension questions.
Instead of grading student work for you, Khanmigo works directly with students to guide their thinking. You get progress reports and insights into where students are struggling.
Several platforms now claim to “grade essays with AI.” We tested a handful and the pattern was consistent: surface-level scoring with generic feedback.
We’re not ready to trust AI to grade essays, and neither should you. Use AI to support your feedback process, not replace your judgment.
The biggest mistake we see? Districts buying one tool and mandating it for everyone. Different teachers need different solutions.
